4. Methods
   To test the theory, I conduct an experiment manipulating whether
employees are held accountable for uncontrollable outcomes (between-
subjects) and the degree to which uncontrollable outcomes provide
decision-relevant information for controllable outcomes (within-subjects).
Individual goal focus is captured after the main task using two different
measures. Importantly, the experiment is constructed such that holding
employees accountable for uncontrollable outcomes gives them weaker
economic incentives to make good decisions. Thus, any observed benefits
point to the information-processing theory proposed in this study.
   The experiment uses a diagnostic learning task in which the optimal
action depends on the unobservable state (customer type). Participants
can learn the state using feedback they receive after each choice. Diag-
nostic learning—where making good decisions requires learning about
an unobservable state parameter—is a hallmark of many important man-
agement problems such as the newsvendor problem (Bolton and Katok
[2008]). In fact, a wide range of important decisions require individuals
to make inferences about unobservable states, such as physicians mak-
ing treatment decisions based on inferences about unobservable patient
condition and auditors choosing audit procedures based on inferences
about unobservable risk levels (Currie and MacLeod [2020]; Hong and
Shields [2022]). The task used to capture diagnostic learning in this
study is conceptually similar to other tasks commonly used in accounting
research (Sprinkle [2000], Hannan, Krishnan, and Newman [2008]) and
closely operationalizes the model developed in Casas-Arce, Lourenço, and
Martínez-Jerez [2017]. However, a key aspect of this study is that feedback
on both controllable and uncontrollable outcomes provides information
about the unknown state. Thus, considering both information sources can
lead to better decisions. The next sections outline the task in more detail.

4.1 the experimental task
  Participants play an economic game in which they work for a hypo-
thetical company that produces cars in three factories (Factory Alpha,
Beta, and Gamma). Participants only make decisions for one factory
(Alpha) and they do not have control over decisions in other two factories
(Beta and Gamma). The economic game consists of three rounds. In each
round, participants choose which model of car to produce in their factory
(Alpha). They can produce one of six models (model A, B, C, D, E, or F)
and they are free to choose the same or different models across choice
rounds. The payoffs from producing each model depend on unobservable
customer preferences (i.e., the unobservable state parameter). In partic-
ular, customers have a preference for one of the models—designated the
winning model. Choosing the wining model generates one point while
choosing any other model generates zero points.3 Participants who learn
the winning model more quickly will receive more compensation because
they are paid for each point they generate (more details in subsection 4.3).
The winning model is randomly determined before the first round and is
the same for the entire game (i.e., all three rounds). Ex ante, each model
has an equal chance to be determined the winning model.
   4.1.1. Learning the Winning Model. Participants can learn the winning
model using trial and error. With their first choice, they can only guess.
If they do not guess the winning model, then they should eliminate that
model and guess a different model with their subsequent choice(s). If they
do guess the winning model, then they should continue to choose that
model with all subsequent choices.4
   Notably, participants can also learn from the two uncontrollable facto-
ries because they are told that the winning model is the same in each fac-
tory for the entire game. Thus, the uncontrollable outcomes in the other
factories provide information about the unobservable state (customer pref-
erences). If losing models are produced in the other factories, then par-
ticipants should eliminate those models and guess different models with
their subsequent choice(s). If the winning model is produced in one of the
other factories, then participants should also choose that model in their
own factory with their subsequent choice(s). For example, imagine that a
participant produces model A in their own factory while models B and C

   3 This scoring system ensures that risk preferences do not play a role in participants’ deci-

sions. If participants learn the winning model, then they should choose that model with all
their remaining choices, regardless of their risk preferences. Similarly, if they learn that an
option is not the winning model, then they should not choose that model with any of their
remaining choices, regardless of their risk preferences.
   4 Participants are not given any information about the probability of each model being

selected as the winning model ex ante. Thus, they likely assume that each model has an equal
chance to be the winning model (Falk and Lann [2008]). Regardless, while subjective beliefs
may influence participants’ guesses before the winning model is revealed, they cannot play a
role in decision quality given that the winning model is uniformly distributed.

are produced in the other factories. If any of the three choices generates
1 point—indicating it is the winning model—then the participant should
produce that model in all remaining rounds. Yet if all three choices gener-
ate 0 points—indicating that none of them are the winning model—then
the participant should eliminate those models and choose model D, E, or F
in the next round. Accordingly, learning from the uncontrollable outcomes
in the other two factories can help participants generate more points in
their own factory. In the previous examples, participants who only pay at-
tention to their own factory will only know whether model A is the winner
or not, whereas those who pay attention to all factories will know whether
models A, B, or C is a winner or not.
   Each participant plays 20 independent trials, or iterations, of the game
such that they make 60 total choices. Their pay depends on the total points
they generate across all choices. The winning model is randomly chosen at
the start of each trial and the random draws are independent across trials.
Thus, participants need to learn anew with each new trial.
  4.1.2. Performance Reports. Participants can learn using the performance
report they receive after each round. The report shows which model was
chosen and how many points were generated in each of the three factories
for the previous choice round (see figure 2). The numbers in the report
are blurred to make them impossible to read unless participants hover over
them with the mouse. Once participants stop hovering, the numbers im-
mediately become blurred again. In both panels of figure 2, participants

                            the (un)controllability principle             665

can currently see the feedback for their own factory because the mouse is
hovered over that section of the performance report. The feedback for the
other factories and for the bonus amounts (discussed in subsection 4.3)
works similarly.
   Requiring participants to hover their mouse to view the numbers makes
it possible capture their attention by tracking how much time they spend
looking at each piece of information. Accordingly, I can precisely measure
whether holding employees accountable for uncontrollable factors (i.e.,
the other factories) affects how much they pay attention to those factors.
   Eleven understanding checks are interspersed throughout the instruc-
tions. One understanding check verifies that participants knew the win-
ning model is the same in each factory and two other checks verify that
participants knew how to read the performance report. Two other atten-
tion checks serve as manipulation checks by assessing whether participants
understood their financial incentives.

   4.1.3. Choices in the Other Factories. The production choices in the other
factories (Beta and Gamma) are made by hypothetical employees using a
computerized algorithm. Using hypothetical employees allows me to en-
sure that the uncontrollable factors are informative on average and to ma-
nipulate the degree to which that feedback is informative (more details in
subsection 4.3). The algorithm underlying the two hypothetical employ-
ees chooses randomly with two restrictions. First, if the winning is model
is found in one of the three factories, then the algorithm will choose that
model in subsequent choices for that trial. Second, the algorithm will not
choose a model that has already been chosen in another factory during that
trial. These restrictions ensure that the hypothetical employees act intelli-
gently. The second restriction is particularly important because it increases
the chances that their choices will be informative to the participant. If they
instead chose models that had already been chosen in one of factories pre-
viously, then those choices would provide no incremental information, as
choosing a model once is enough to learn its value (either 0 or 1). Partici-
pants are told that choices for the other factories are made by hypothetical
employees. However, they are not told how those choices are made because
doing so would reveal the optimal strategy that participants are tasked with
discovering.


4.2 dependent variable
  To test the hypotheses, the quality of participants’ decision-making is
measured based on whether or not they chose the winning model in their
own factory in a given round. As stated previously, participants who learn
more from the outcomes in the two uncontrollable factories will be able
to identify the state parameter and choose the winning model more often.
There are 60 observations for each participant corresponding to their 60
choices ( = 3 rounds * 20 trials).

4.3 independent variables
   The low versus more controllable measure: Whether participants are held ac-
countable for uncontrollable factors is manipulated by randomly assigning
them to be paid either based on the more or less controllable measure.
Participants evaluated on the more controllable measure receive $0.08 for
every point they generate in their own factory while those evaluated on
the less controllable measure receive $0.04 for every point they generate
in their own factory and $0.02 for every point generated in the other two
factories.5 Thus, participants evaluated on the more controllable measure
are paid based only on performance in their own factory. In contrast, those
evaluated on the less controllable measure are paid based on performance
in all factories.
   Participants can see their pay by examining the performance reports they
receive after each choice. The bottom row of the report shows how much
pay they received from each factory. To the right of the report, they see the
total pay they earned for the current round and across all rounds thus far.
Figure 2, panel A (respectively, panel B), shows an example performance
report for participants evaluated on the more (respectively, less) control-
lable measure.
   Note that participants evaluated on the more controllable measure have
stronger economic incentives to work hard because their pay depends more
on how well they make decisions for their factory. Although participants
can always submit uniformed guesses, effort can still play an important role
because acquiring and processing information in the performance reports
takes time and energy (Stone and Ziebart [1995], Sprinkle [2000]). Given
that the more controllable measure provides stronger economic incentives,
standard theory suggests that it should make participants more likely to
expend the necessary effort to consider all the available information—
including information for uncontrollable factors. Yet, due to goal-focused
information processing, my theory suggests that those with the more con-
trollable measure will exhibit tunnel vision, making them less likely to con-
sider the information for uncontrollable factories.6

5 Note that $0.02 is used because there are two other factories (2*$0.02 = $0.04). This

amount holds constant the range of possible payoffs across conditions.
    6 One argument against holding employees accountable for uncontrollable factors is that

it can expose them to additional risk. Yet this argument does not necessarily apply in the cur-
rent experimental setup because the less controllable measure may expose employees to less
risk than the more controllable measure (due to risk sharing with the other divisions’ perfor-
mance). Importantly, however, the strategy that maximizes participants’ expected utility in this
experiment is the same regardless of risk preferences (see footnote 3) and participants evalu-
ated on the more controllable measure still have stronger economic incentives to make good
decisions because their pay is more sensitive to their own decisions compared to participants
evaluated on the less controllable measure.

5. Results
   The study was completed by 301 participants recruited on Amazon’s
Mechanical Turk.10,11 After dropping 21 participants who did not answer
both manipulation checks correctly, the final sample consist of 280 partic-
ipants.12 Using Mechanical Turk participants is appropriate because I use
an abstract decision-making task that requires no special skills or knowl-
edge. Participants spent an average of 19.70 minutes on the experiment
and earned average hourly pay of $8.85. To improve data quality, I (1) re-
quire participants to complete a CAPTCHA verification on the first page,
(2) only recruit workers in the United States who have completed at least
100 HITs with an approval rating of at least 95%, (3) use CloudResearch to
“Block Low Quality Participants” (Eyal et al. [2021]), and (4) use the “Pre-
vent multiple submissions” setting in Qualtrics. Table 1 provides descriptive
statistics for the variables used in tabulated analyses.

Board.

once, 24 data entries had duplicate MTurk worker IDs. These observations are dropped from

observations for participants who started but did not finish the task. Among this group, 13
never saw the manipulation. The number of workers who started but did not finish the study
did not differ across conditions (p = 0.638). This procedure results in the final sample of 301
participants.
